passages.t: ‘I was glad when they said to me, Let us go to the house of the LORD’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A song of ascents. Of David” (verse 1). The singer remembers the invitation. “I was glad when they said to me, ‘Let us go to the house of the LORD’” (verse 1).

Now he has arrived. “Our feet are standing in your gates, O Jerusalem” (verse 2). He looks at the city. “Jerusalem is built up as a city united together” (verse 3). It is the place “where the tribes go up, the tribes of the LORD, as a testimony for Israel, to give thanks to the name of the LORD” (verse 4). “For there the thrones of judgment stand, the thrones of the house of David” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Psalm 121 was the road. Psalm 122 is the arrival. The note on Psalm 120 explains the Songs of Ascents and the pilgrims who went up to Jerusalem for the feasts.

Imagine a family from a farming village, after days of walking, standing at last inside the gates of the great city. They had never seen walls so thick, or towers so tall, or so many people of their own nation in one place. ‘Our feet are standing’ is the sound of someone catching his breath.

‘United together’ (verse 3) may describe the city packed tightly on its ridge within its walls. It may also describe the people it gathered: tribes from every part of the land, joined as one in worship.

Jerusalem was the place of worship and also the place of justice. The ‘thrones of judgment’ (verse 5) were where the king of David's line heard cases. In Israel the king was meant to be the final court and the protector of the weak. Worship and justice belonged together in the same city.

‘Of David’ in the heading may mean written by David, or belonging to a collection linked with him. The book page explains the question. Many scholars think the psalm was written later, after the temple was built.
passages.later:
Jesus' family went up to Jerusalem each year for Passover (Luke 2:41). As a man, he too came up to the city and its temple at the feasts.

Hebrews tells believers that they have come to another Jerusalem: “you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews 12:22).
passages.asks:
‘I was glad when they said to me, Let us go to the house of the LORD.’ Is worship with God's people something you are glad to go to, or something you put up with? The psalm does not scold. It simply remembers joy.

Notice too that someone said ‘Let us go.’ The pilgrim did not go alone. Who invited you to God? Who might you invite?

passages.happening:
Now the pilgrim calls others to pray. “Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: ‘May those who love you prosper. May there be peace within your walls, and prosperity inside your fortresses’” (verses 6 and 7).

He prays it himself, and he gives his reasons. “For the sake of my brothers and friends, I will say, ‘Peace be within you’” (verse 8). “For the sake of the house of the LORD our God, I will seek your prosperity” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The Hebrew word for ‘peace’ is shalom. It comes three times here (verses 6, 7 and 8). Shalom is more than the absence of war. It means everything being whole and well: safety, health, fairness, enough to eat, people living rightly with each other and with God. A first hearer would also catch the sound of the city's name, Jerusalem, which in Hebrew sounds a little like shalom. The singer prays for the city to become what its name sounds like.

Notice the two reasons. The first is people: ‘my brothers and friends’, the neighbours who live there and the pilgrims who come. The second is God: ‘the house of the LORD’. Love for God and love for neighbour lead to the same prayer.

Psalm 120 ended with a man who wanted peace among people who wanted war. Psalm 122 ends with a prayer for peace in the city of God.
passages.later:
When Jesus came near Jerusalem for the last time, he wept over the city and said, “If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace!” (Luke 19:42).

God told his people in exile in Babylon to pray even for a foreign city: “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf” (Jeremiah 29:7). And Jesus said, “Blessed are the peacemakers” (Matthew 5:9).
passages.hard: Verse 6 is often quoted today in arguments about the modern city and the modern state. These notes make no claim about any modern state, government, border or conflict, and nothing here is said against any people who live in that land. In its own setting the psalm is a pilgrim's prayer for the city of the temple. Christians apply it in different ways: some pray for the city of Jerusalem itself and all who live there; others read it chiefly of the heavenly Jerusalem and God's people everywhere; many hold both. Whatever a reader draws from it, the psalm asks for shalom, which includes justice and the good of neighbours. It is a prayer anyone may pray for a city and its people. Its words cannot be used to bless hatred or harm.
passages.asks:
Whose peace do you pray for? You may pray this psalm for Jerusalem and for everyone who lives there. You may also pray it for your own town, your church, your street, and the people you find hardest to love.

Shalom is not only something to pray for. Verse 9 says, ‘I will seek your prosperity.’ Prayer for peace leads to work for peace.
